messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Boonsong Rattanakit is a sixty-year-old Thai-American fisherman who has lived on the Gulf Coast of Louisiana for the better part of three decades. He came to the United States as a young man, built a modest but stable life alongside his wife and a small community of Southeast Asian fishing families, and found in the rhythms of the water something close to peace. That peace was shattered roughly eight months ago when his younger brother, who had been working alongside him on the boat, was pulled overboard during a sudden squall. Boonsong was at the helm when it happened. He saw his brother go over the rail. By the time he had brought the vessel around and thrown the ring buoy, his brother had already been taken under by the current. The Coast Guard recovered the body two days later. Boonsong was on the dock when they brought him in.

In the weeks that followed, Boonsong returned to work because he did not know what else to do with himself. The boat, the water, the early morning smell of diesel and brine — all of it had become a landscape of unbearable association. When the hull pitched in choppy water, even mildly, his body responded as though the squall had returned: his heart hammered, his hands went cold and rigid on the wheel, his chest locked around a breath he could not release. These physical reactions were not merely uncomfortable; they confirmed something he had already begun to believe. He had come to feel, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that he was guilty of surviving — that he had been at the helm, that he had not moved fast enough, that some essential failure of his had cost his brother his life. This belief that he bore responsibility for the death, that he was in some fundamental sense culpable, sat beneath every waking hour and fed directly into the state of vigilance his body seemed unable to leave. The guilt and the shame kept the threat alive; his nervous system remained on permanent alert, scanning the water, the weather, the faces of the other men on the dock, as though catastrophe were always seconds away.

What made this worse — and what he found hardest to articulate to anyone, including his wife — was that the physical alarm his body sounded each morning on the water seemed to confirm the appraisals rather than simply accompany them. When his hands shook at the wheel, he interpreted this not as a symptom of grief but as evidence: his body knew what he had done. The strong negative feelings — the horror that surfaced without warning when he saw a life ring hanging on a dock post, the shame that rose when a fellow fisherman mentioned his brother's name — these emotions felt to Boonsong like verdicts rather than reactions. Each surge of fear or guilt reinforced his certainty that he was a man who could not be trusted with the lives of others, and that the world had confirmed this.

Over the months, Boonsong had grown quieter and more withdrawn. He described feeling dead inside — not sad exactly, but hollowed, as though the part of him that had once taken pleasure in the catch, in his wife's cooking, in the company of the men he had known for decades, had simply stopped functioning. He had come to believe that people, broadly, could not be trusted — not out of paranoia exactly, but out of a kind of exhausted disillusionment, a sense that proximity to him carried risk. He had pulled back from the small community of Thai and Vietnamese fishermen who had been his social world, declining invitations, deflecting conversation. His wife had told him, carefully and more than once, that she was frightened by how far away he seemed.

Sleep had become unreliable, fractured by waking in the early hours with his heart already racing, the room dark and unfamiliar for a disorienting moment. He sought help now because his wife had finally said plainly that she could not watch him disappear. What he feared most, sitting in the intake chair, was not the memories themselves but the possibility that the man he had been before the squall was simply gone.
